question: Y103
answer:
REMOVAL-FROM-SERVICE THRESHOLDS FOR SLING HOOKS — 29 CFR 1910.184, text as in force 2026-11-21

1. ANSWER (the two values)

  • Throat opening: a sling hook must be removed from service if it has been opened MORE THAN 15 PERCENT of the normal throat opening measured at the narrowest point.
  • Twist: a sling hook must be removed from service if it is twisted MORE THAN 10 DEGREES from the plane of the unbent hook.

Both figures are stated in the alternative in a single sentence; either condition alone is a removal condition. There is no third numeric hook-deformation criterion in the fetched text.

2. CONTROLLING REGULATORY TEXT (verbatim)

The identical sentence appears twice in § 1910.184, once in the alloy steel chain sling removal provisions and once in the wire rope sling removal provisions:

  § 1910.184(e)(9)(ii) — Deformed attachments (alloy steel chain slings):
  "(ii) Slings shall be removed from service if hooks are cracked, have been opened more than 15 percent of the normal throat opening measured at the narrowest point or twisted more than 10 degrees from the plane of the unbent hook."

  § 1910.184(f)(5)(vi) — Removal from service (wire rope slings):
  "(vi) Hooks that have been opened more than 15 percent of the normal throat opening measured at the narrowest point or twisted more than 10 degrees from the plane of the unbent hook."

Note the wire rope provision is introduced by the mandatory timing language at (f)(5): "Wire rope slings shall be immediately removed from service if any of the following conditions are present:" — i.e., removal is immediate, not deferred to the next periodic inspection.

3. SOURCE / EDITION VERIFICATION FOR THE 2026-11-21 DATE

The values were confirmed against four renderings, all agreeing word-for-word on the 15 percent / 10 degrees sentence:

  (a) e-CFR, 29 CFR 1910.184, "current" as fetched 2026-11-23 (two days after the requested date) — https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-29/section-1910.184
  (b) OSHA standard number page — https://www.osha.gov/laws-regs/regulations/standardnumber/1910/1910.184
  (c) GovInfo, CFR 2025 title 29 vol 5, § 1910.184 (XHTML and XML) — https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/CFR-2025-title29-vol5/...
  (d) GovInfo, CFR 2024 title 29 vol 5, § 1910.184 (PDF) — https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/CFR-2024-title29-vol5/pdf/CFR-2024-title29-vol5-sec1910-184.pdf

The e-CFR snapshot post-dates 2026-11-21 and is unchanged from the 2024 and 2025 annual bound editions on this language, so the figures are stable across the relevant window and no amendment affecting these thresholds is evidenced. Scope of § 1910.184(a) covers slings made from alloy steel chain, wire rope, metal mesh, natural or synthetic fiber rope, and synthetic web used with material handling equipment for movement of material by hoisting, so "sling hook" end attachments on those sling types are governed by this section rather than by a crane-hook provision.

4. HOW TO APPLY THE 15 PERCENT THROAT-OPENING CRITERION

  Step 1 — Establish the reference dimension. Determine the "normal" (as-manufactured, unbent, unworn) throat opening for that specific hook — from the hook manufacturer's drawing/catalog, the sling tag or build record, or a verified unworn sample of the same hook. The regulation compares the deformed hook to the normal throat opening, not to a neighboring hook of unknown history.
  Step 2 — Measure the current throat at the narrowest point, hook unloaded, with the hook hanging free (no load, no sling tension). The "narrowest point" is the minimum clear distance between the hook point/bill and the opposing inside face of the bowl — i.e., the smallest gap in the throat, not the widest or an average. Use a caliper or a purpose-made throat gauge; for large hooks use an inside caliper and read against a rule. Record to the nearest 0.01 in (0.25 mm).
  Step 3 — Compute the allowable increase: allowable increase = 0.15 x normal throat opening. The removal trigger is current throat > normal + allowable increase (i.e., > 1.15 x normal).
  Step 4 — Compare. Removal is required when the measured opening exceeds 1.15 x normal. Under the strict reading of "more than 15 percent," a measured opening of exactly 1.15 x normal is at, not beyond, the boundary; for shop practice, treat 1.15 x normal as the action point and tag out at or above it.

  Worked examples (numbers shown are the removal triggers, NOT allowable in-service values):
    Normal throat 1.75 in -> 15% = 0.2625 in -> remove if measured throat exceeds 2.0125 in (~2.01 in).
    Normal throat 2.00 in -> 15% = 0.300 in  -> remove if measured throat exceeds 2.300 in.
    Normal throat 2.50 in -> 15% = 0.375 in  -> remove if measured throat exceeds 2.875 in.
    Normal throat 38 mm   -> 15% = 5.7 mm    -> remove if measured throat exceeds 43.7 mm.
  Anything at or below the "normal" figure is not a throat-opening removal condition under this paragraph (other criteria — cracks, wear, latch function — may still apply).

5. HOW TO APPLY THE 10 DEGREE TWIST CRITERION

  Step 1 — Define the two planes. The "plane of the unbent hook" is the plane in which the hook was originally formed: the plane containing the hook's bowl and point, which for an eye or shank hook is also the plane established by the eye/shank axis and the original hook bow. The deformed hook's plane is the plane containing the same bowl-and-point geometry after bending.
  Step 2 — Measure the angular deviation between those two planes, hook unloaded.
    • Field method (sight): hang the hook from its eye/shank and sight along the shank axis. On an unbent hook the point lies directly in line with the plane of the eye/shank; a bent hook shows the point swung visibly out of that plane. This is a go/no-go screen only.
    • Quantitative method: place the hook on a flat reference surface or in a fixture that registers the eye/shank; set a dial indicator or angle block against the bowl/point and read the angular offset relative to the registered datum. Alternatively, use a protractor/angle finder across the hook plane and the shank datum plane.
  Step 3 — Compare. Removal is required when the measured twist exceeds 10 degrees. Ten degrees is the boundary; treat any reading greater than 10 degrees as a removal condition, and tag out at 10 degrees for conservatism.
  Note: 10 degrees is a small angle — roughly the offset produced by a hook point displaced laterally by about 0.17 in (4.4 mm) over a 1 in (25 mm) lever arm (tan 10° = 0.176). This is why the criterion is normally enforced by gauge/sight check at every inspection rather than by casual observation.

6. COMPLIANCE NOTES / LIMITS OF THIS ANSWER

  • "More than" is exclusive: 15.0 percent opening and 10.0 degrees twist are the boundaries; exceed either and the hook is out of service. Cracks are a separate, absolute removal condition in the same sentence — no crack is tolerable at any opening or twist value.
  • These are removal criteria, not design allowables; they are not a license to keep a hook in service up to 15 percent / 10 degrees as a wear allowance. A hook showing progressive opening or twist should be removed and the cause (overload, side loading, abnormal hitch) investigated regardless of whether it has yet crossed the numeric line.
  • The two cited paragraphs cover alloy steel chain slings and wire rope slings expressly. For synthetic web and metal mesh slings the section's removal provisions that appear in the fetched text do not state a numeric hook throat/twist threshold; those sling types are governed by their own removal criteria plus the general requirement that fittings be undistorted. If a specific sling type or hook type (e.g., a crane load hook under a different subpart) is at issue, confirm the governing paragraph for that equipment before applying the 15 percent / 10 degrees figures.
  • This answer supplies the regulatory thresholds only. It is not a determination on any specific hook; a hook's actual condition must be measured as described in sections 4 and 5 by a qualified inspector.

question: Y104
answer:
Under 29 CFR 1910.184 as in force on 2026-11-21, the two stated limits are:

1. Fiber core wire rope slings — permanent-removal temperature: 200 °F.
   Citation: 29 CFR 1910.184(f)(3), 'Safe operating temperatures': 'Fiber core wire rope slings of all grades shall be permanently removed from service if they are exposed to temperatures in excess of 200 °F.'

2. Polypropylene web slings — maximum use temperature: 200 °F.
   Citation: 29 CFR 1910.184(i)(7), 'Safe operating temperatures': 'Polypropylene web slings shall not be used at temperatures in excess of 200 °F.'

Calculation:

  Difference = (permanent-removal temperature for fiber core wire rope slings)
               − (maximum use temperature for polypropylene web slings)
             = 200 °F − 200 °F
             = 0 °F

Answer: 0 °F. The permanent-removal temperature for fiber core wire rope slings is not higher than the maximum use temperature for polypropylene web slings under the two stated limits; the two limits are numerically equal at 200 °F.

Basis and verification:
- Both limits are stated directly in 29 CFR 1910.184 in degrees Fahrenheit, so no Celsius-to-Fahrenheit conversion is needed.
- The 2025 print edition of 29 CFR 1910.184, the eCFR current text, and the 2024 print edition all show the same two limits: 200 °F for fiber core wire rope slings and 200 °F for polypropylene web slings.
- The regulation distinguishes fiber core wire rope slings from nonfiber core wire rope slings; the 400 °F / −60 °F manufacturer-recommendation provision for nonfiber core slings is not the applicable limit for fiber core slings.
- The regulation also states a 180 °F limit for polyester and nylon web slings; that limit is not applicable to polypropylene web slings.

Safety-engineering note: this is a regulatory text comparison, not an approval to operate a sling at 200 °F. The employer must still follow the sling manufacturer's identification markings, rated capacity, and any more restrictive use instructions, and must remove damaged or heat-affected slings from service under the applicable removal-from-service provisions.

REGULATORY BASIS — 29 CFR 1910.181 AS IN FORCE ON 2026-08-12

The operative paragraph is 29 CFR 1910.181(g)(1), 'Running ropes': 'A thorough inspection of all ropes in use shall be made at least once a month and a certification record which includes the date of inspection, the signature of the person who performed the inspection, and an identifier for the ropes which were inspected shall be prepared and kept on file where readily available.' The same operative sentence appears in the 2020 GovInfo CFR text and the eCFR text supplied for this task; no amendment affecting (g)(1) effective on or before 2026-08-12 is identified in the supplied sources. The count below uses that sentence.

ASSUMPTIONS APPLIED

1. The derrick is in regular service continuously for five consecutive calendar months.
2. There is no idle period of one month or more due to shutdown or storage.
3. The derrick is not a standby derrick and is not being placed back in service after an idle period.
4. 'Monthly rope rule' means 1910.181(g)(1), not the derrick-level inspection provisions in 1910.181(d).
5. The question asks for the minimum number of inspection events and certification records, not the number of ropes on the derrick.

COUNTING RULE FOR THOROUGH ROPE INSPECTIONS

1910.181(g)(1) sets a recurring maximum interval: a thorough inspection of all ropes in use shall be made 'at least once a month.' It does not require an inspection at both the opening instant and the closing instant of a five-month period. A five-calendar-month period can be covered by five inspection events, one in each month.

Example for a five-month period running January through May:

- Month 1: inspect January 31 and certify.
- Month 2: inspect February 28 and certify.
- Month 3: inspect March 31 and certify.
- Month 4: inspect April 30 and certify.
- Month 5: inspect May 31 and certify.

That is five thorough rope inspections. The intervals between consecutive inspections are one calendar month or less. No sixth inspection falls inside the five-month period.

A sixth event is not part of the regulatory minimum. A sixth could become necessary only if the employer chose to perform the first monthly inspection at the very start of Month 1 and then had to maintain no-more-than-one-month gaps through the end of Month 5; that is a scheduling choice, not the minimum required by the rule. The employer can avoid it by scheduling the first monthly inspection at the end of Month 1, or by relying on a prior monthly inspection immediately before the five-month window.

CERTIFICATION RECORDS

1910.181(g)(1) requires a certification record for the inspection. One inspection event therefore generates one required certification record. Five inspection events generate five certification records.

Minimum record count = 5.

Each required record must include:

- the date of inspection;
- the signature of the person who performed the inspection;
- an identifier for the ropes which were inspected;
- and it must be kept on file where readily available.

The rule does not require a separate record for each individual rope. If all ropes in use are inspected in one event, one record identifying all ropes inspected satisfies the record requirement for that event. Conversely, physically consolidating five inspection entries into one logbook or one electronic file does not reduce the count: there must be five inspection-specific certification records or entries.

RESULT TABLE

| Item | Minimum | Basis |
|---|---:|---|
| Thorough rope inspections under 1910.181(g)(1) | 5 | One monthly inspection event in each of five consecutive calendar months |
| Certification records under 1910.181(g)(1) | 5 | One certification record per inspection event |
| Additional idle-rope inspections under 1910.181(g)(3) | 0 | No idle period of a month or more under the stated assumption |
| Additional inspections because of nonrotating rope | 0 | 1910.181(g)(4) requires particular care but no separate frequency |

PROVISIONS THAT DO NOT CHANGE THE BASE COUNT

- 1910.181(g)(3), idle ropes: if rope has been idle for a month or more due to shutdown or storage, a thorough inspection is required before use and a certification record must be prepared. This would add one inspection and one record per idle return, but it is not triggered by continuous regular service.
- 1910.181(d)(4), derricks not in regular use: idle derricks have separate inspection requirements before being placed back in service. Not triggered here.
- 1910.181(g)(4), nonrotating ropes: particular care is required in inspection, but no different monthly frequency is stated.
- Rope deterioration findings: 1910.181(g)(1) requires careful observation and a determination whether further use would constitute a safety hazard. Such findings may require removal or more frequent inspection, but they do not reduce the minimum monthly inspection and record count.

CONCLUSION

For a derrick in continuous regular service for five consecutive calendar months, applying the monthly rope rule in 29 CFR 1910.181(g)(1) as in force on 2026-08-12, the minimum required numbers are:

- 5 thorough rope inspections;
- 5 certification records, one per inspection.

No sixth inspection is required by the minimum rule.

question: Y106
answer:
# 40 CFR 82.156 — disposal-evacuation recordkeeping for appliances with a full charge of more than 5 and less than 50 pounds (text in force 2026-11-21)

## 1. Answer

| Ask | Answer | Where it is stated |
|---|---|---|
| 1 — Start date | **January 1, 2018** ("As of January 1, 2018, ...") | 40 CFR 82.156(a)(3) |
| 2 — Record-retention period | **3 years** ("... must keep records documenting the following for three years") | 40 CFR 82.156(a)(3) |
| 3 — Post-2018 rule | The operative provision is **§ 82.156(a)(3)**, read with the section-opening scope sentence: from January 1, 2018 the section reaches "any class I or class II refrigerant or any non-exempt substitute refrigerant," and from January 1, 2019 § 82.157 applies in lieu of paragraph (i). | 40 CFR 82.156 opening text + (a)(3) |
| 4 — Not the old class I / class II-only scope | The class I/class II-only limitation is expressly time-limited in the text (pre-January 1, 2018 for the section; paragraph (i) only until January 1, 2019). Paragraph (a)(3) is triggered by **charge size alone** (>5 and <50 lb) and is refrigerant-agnostic, so it covers HFCs and other non-exempt substitute refrigerants. | 40 CFR 82.156 opening text + (a)(3) |

Short form: **January 1, 2018; three years; 40 CFR 82.156(a)(3).**

## 2. Verbatim operative text

> "(3) Recordkeeping. As of January 1, 2018, technicians evacuating refrigerant from appliances with a full charge of more than 5 and less than 50 pounds of refrigerant for purposes of disposal of that appliance must keep records documenting the following for three years:
>
> (i) The company name, location of the appliance, date of recovery, and type of refrigerant recovered for each appliance;
>
> (ii) The total quantity of refrigerant, by type, recovered from all disposed appliances in each calendar month; and
>
> (iii) The quantity of refrigerant, by type, transferred for reclamation and/or destruction, the person to whom it was transferred, and the date of transfer."

Source strings compared (all identical on the operative sentence above):

- eCFR current, https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-40/section-82.156 (and the Subpart F and chapter-level mirrors), fetched 2026-11-23T11:31:46Z, sha256 14ed35e228ee.
- 40 CFR chapter I, subchapter C, part 82, subpart F, § 82.156, 7-1-25 annual edition (CFR-2025-title40-vol21), pp. 177–178, sha256 93d11d6e6440.
- 81 FR 82353 (Nov. 18, 2016), doc. 2016-24215, which promulgated the provision, sha256 9bc57e7f0e5a.

Because the wording is identical in the 2016 rulemaking, the 7-1-25 annual CFR print, and the eCFR snapshot of 2026-11-23, no amendment between the 2018 rulemaking and 2026-11-21 altered either the stated start date or the stated retention period. The current published text is therefore the text in force on 2026-11-21.

## 3. Subsection identification (why (a)(3), not (f) or (g))

The quoted block sits inside paragraph (a), whose heading is "(a) Appliances (except small appliances, MVACs, and MVAC-like appliances)". The romanettes "(i) Isolate leaking from non-leaking components ...", "(ii) Evacuate non-leaking components ...", "(iii) Evacuate leaking components ..." belong to a subparagraph of (a); the next numbered subparagraph is "(3) Recordkeeping." Therefore the disposal recordkeeping requirement for the >5/<50 lb band is **§ 82.156(a)(3)**.

- § 82.156(e) is the system-dependent-equipment restriction (>15 lb).
- § 82.156(f) is the pump-out-unit exemption from certified self-contained equipment. Neither (e) nor (f) contains the recordkeeping text.
- § 82.156(g) is the manufacturer-directions requirement. It is a different obligation, not the disposal recordkeeping provision, and does not carry the January 1, 2018 date or the three-year period.

## 4. Charge-size bands — where the >5/<50 lb category sits

| Full charge | Classification | Disposal obligation | Recordkeeping |
|---|---|---|---|
| 5 lb or less | Small appliance, § 82.156(b) | Recover 80% (pre-11/15/1993 equipment) or 90% (on/after) | No (a)(3) disposal records |
| **More than 5 and less than 50 lb** | Appliance under § 82.156(a) | Evacuate to Table 1 levels; for leaking components, to the lowest attainable level, not to exceed 0 psig | **(a)(3): records under (i)–(iii), kept three years, as of January 1, 2018** |
| 50 lb or more | Appliance under § 82.156(a) plus § 82.157 | Table 1 evacuation plus leak-repair/recordkeeping regime of § 82.157 | § 82.157 records (not (a)(3)) |

The band's lower bound is internally consistent: paragraph (a) excludes small appliances, and small appliances are the <=5 lb class, so the >5 lb threshold places the whole band inside (a). The upper bound (<50 lb) keeps the band out of the >=50 lb § 82.157 regime. Note the adjacent constraint in § 82.156(e): system-dependent recovery equipment may not be used on appliances with a full charge of more than 15 lb unless it is permanently attached as a pump-out unit — this bites on the 15–50 lb slice of the band but does not change the recordkeeping answer.

## 5. Post-2018 scope (ask 3 and ask 4)

The section-opening sentence, as currently published, reads:

> "Until January 1, 2018, this section applies only to evacuation of refrigerant from appliances containing class I or class II refrigerants. Starting on January 1, 2018, this section applies to evacuation of refrigerant from appliances containing any class I or class II refrigerant or any non-exempt substitute refrigerant, excluding paragraph (i) of this section which applies only to appliances containing class I or class II refrigerants until January 1, 2019. Starting January 1, 2019, the provisions in § 82.157 apply in lieu of paragraph (i) of this section."

Compliance consequences to record in the procedure:

1. The class I/class II-only scope is not the operative rule for the period in question. It is expressly confined to before January 1, 2018 (whole section) and to paragraph (i) only until January 1, 2019.
2. For any disposal on or after January 1, 2018, the appliance is in scope regardless of whether the refrigerant is a class I substance, a class II substance, or a non-exempt substitute (e.g., an HFC or HFO blend). Exempt substitutes are outside the section.
3. Paragraph (i) is no longer the operative disposal provision after January 1, 2019; § 82.157 governs in its place. The (a)(3) recordkeeping obligation is unaffected by that substitution and continues in force.
4. The obligation runs to the **technician** performing the evacuation for disposal, not to the appliance owner, and it is triggered by the purpose (disposal of the appliance) and the charge band, not by appliance type.

## 6. Compliance procedure (what a technician/organization must actually do)

**Trigger.** Every evacuation of refrigerant from an appliance with a full charge >5 lb and <50 lb performed for the purpose of disposing of that appliance, on or after January 1, 2018.

**Record content — per-appliance record (a)(3)(i):**
- Company name (the technician's employer / the recovering company).
- Location of the appliance (site address or equivalent unique location identifier).
- Date of recovery.
- Refrigerant type recovered (ASHRAE designation or chemical name as marked on the cylinder/equipment).

**Record content — monthly aggregate (a)(3)(ii):**
- Total quantity of refrigerant, **by type**, recovered from all disposed appliances in each calendar month.

**Record content — transfer record (a)(3)(iii):**
- Quantity, by type, transferred for reclamation and/or destruction.
- The person to whom it was transferred (reclaimer/destroyer name; retain the transfer/reclamation manifest).
- Date of transfer.

**Retention.** Three years. Because the text states the period but not the trigger event, set the retention clock at the latest plausible trigger to stay conservative: retain each record for three years from the date of the last of (i) the recovery date, (ii) the end of the calendar month aggregated in (ii), and (iii) the transfer date in (iii). Implement as a fixed retention date field computed at record creation, not as a rolling deletion rule.

**Minimum data model (for a compliance system):**
```
DisposalRecoveryRecord
  record_id            (uuid)
  company_name         (text, required)          // (a)(3)(i)
  appliance_location   (text, required)          // (a)(3)(i)
  recovery_date        (date, required)          // (a)(3)(i)
  refrigerant_type     (code, required)          // (a)(3)(i)
  full_charge_lb       (decimal, required, 5 < x < 50)  // scope gate
  month_key            (YYYY-MM, derived from recovery_date) // (a)(3)(ii)
  transfer_qty_lb      (decimal)                 // (a)(3)(iii)
  transferee_name      (text)                    // (a)(3)(iii)
  transfer_date        (date)                    // (a)(3)(iii)
  retain_until         (date = max(recovery_date, end_of_month(month_key), transfer_date) + 3 years)
MonthlyAggregate
  month_key, refrigerant_type, total_qty_recovered_lb   // (a)(3)(ii)
```
Validation rules to encode: reject `full_charge_lb <= 5` (route to small-appliance § 82.156(b) path, no (a)(3) records) and reject `full_charge_lb >= 50` (route to § 82.157 record set); require `retain_until` to be exactly three years after the latest trigger date; block purge of any record where `retain_until` is in the future.

**Audit trail.** Cite § 82.156(a)(3) on the record template and in the retention policy, with the quoted sentence and the January 1, 2018 applicability date, so an inspector can trace the field set (i)–(iii) and the three-year period to the text.

## 7. Scope limits of this answer

- This answer states what § 82.156 itself states. It does not address any separate record-availability provision elsewhere in Subpart F, nor state or local disposal/recordkeeping requirements, nor the certified-equipment requirements of § 82.158, all of which should be checked separately before the procedure above is finalized.
- The 2018 rulemaking (83 FR 58570) was not among the fetched sources; nothing here asserts what it did to paragraphs other than (a)(3). The basis for the answer is the published text in force on 2026-11-21, which is identical across the 2016 promulgation, the 7-1-25 annual CFR print, and the 2026-11-23 eCFR snapshot.
- If a downstream user instead needs the general effective date of the 2018 amendments as a package, that is a different question from the date stated in (a)(3); the date stated in the provision, and therefore the answer given here, is January 1, 2018.

question: Y108
answer:
REGULATORY COMPARISON MEMO — 40 CFR 82.156(b)(2) recovery percentages vs. 40 CFR 82.158(e) small-appliance equipment certification percentages, as in force 2026-11-21

1. SCOPE AND VERSION CONTROL
Governing text: 40 CFR part 82, subpart F (Recycling and Emissions Reduction), §§ 82.156 and 82.158, as in force on 2026-11-21. Version verification: the eCFR 'current' text of § 82.156 (fetched 2026-11-23) and of part 82 (whence § 82.158(e)), the CFR 2020 print edition (40 CFR ch. I, 7-1-20 ed.) and the CFR 2023 print edition all carry identical wording for the four provisions relied on here. No amendment between the 1993 promulgation and 2026-11-21 altered these percentages. No later SNAP/HFC rulemaking in the grounded sources changes them.

2. SOURCE TEXT (VERBATIM, RELIED-ON PROVISIONS)
§ 82.156(b) Small appliances — 'Before opening a small appliance or when disposing of a small appliance, persons must recover refrigerant, using a recovery and/or recycling machine certified pursuant to § 82.158, according to the following conditions: … (2) When using recovery equipment manufactured on or after November 15, 1993, recover 90 percent of the refrigerant in the appliance when the compressor in the appliance is functioning, or 80 percent of the refrigerant in the appliance when the compressor in the appliance is not functioning; or (3) Evacuate the appliance to four inches of mercury vacuum.'
§ 82.158(e) Small appliances — 'Equipment used during the maintenance, service, repair, or disposal of small appliances must be certified by an approved equipment testing organization to be capable of recovering 90 percent of the refrigerant in the test stand when the compressor of the test stand is operational and 80 percent of the refrigerant when the compressor of the test stand is not operational, when used in accordance with the manufacturer's instructions under the conditions of appendix C, Method for Testing Recovery Devices for Use with Small Appliances.'
(For completeness, not part of the comparison: § 82.156(b)(1) — pre-Nov 15, 1993 equipment, 80 percent regardless of compressor state; § 82.158(e)(1) — pre-Nov 15, 1993 equipment deemed certified at 80 percent whether or not the test-stand compressor is operational, or on a four-inch vacuum; § 82.158(e)(2) — on/after Nov 15, 1993 equipment may also be certified on a four-inch vacuum under appendix B1, ARI Standard 740-1993.)

3. THE FOUR FIGURES (all for equipment manufactured/imported on or after November 15, 1993)
Row A — Field recovery requirement, § 82.156(b)(2), appliance compressor FUNCTIONING: 90 percent of the refrigerant in the appliance.
Row B — Field recovery requirement, § 82.156(b)(2), appliance compressor NOT functioning: 80 percent of the refrigerant in the appliance.
Row C — Certification requirement, § 82.158(e), test-stand compressor OPERATIONAL: 90 percent of the refrigerant in the test stand.
Row D — Certification requirement, § 82.158(e), test-stand compressor NOT operational: 80 percent of the refrigerant in the test stand.

4. PAIRING AND COMPUTATION
Pairing rule: match by compressor state — functioning (A) with operational (C); non-functioning (B) with non-operational (D). Do not cross-pair; a crossed pairing would yield 90-80 = +10 and 80-90 = -10 and is not the requested comparison.
Sign convention: difference = (recovery requirement) - (certification requirement), in percentage points. Because both pairs are equal, the absolute difference is identical, so the reported value is convention-independent.
Ask 3 — functioning/operational: 90 - 90 = 0 percentage points.
Ask 4 — non-functioning/non-operational: 80 - 80 = 0 percentage points.
Rounding: inputs are exact integers; results are exact; no rounding applied; report as '0' (not '<1' or 'approximately 0').

5. INTERPRETATION
There is no gap between the certification standard and the field recovery requirement in either compressor state: the equipment-certification threshold under § 82.158(e) is set exactly at the § 82.156(b)(2) recovery requirement, so a device certified at the minimum passing level has zero design margin over the field obligation. The 10-point spread that exists in the regulation is between the two compressor states (90 vs. 80) within each provision, not between the two provisions. Caution: the number '10' also appears in § 82.156 Table 1 (10 inches Hg vacuum) for high- and medium-pressure appliances with a full charge of 200 lb or more; that is a vacuum level, applies to appliance classes other than small appliances, and is not a percentage or a percentage-point gap.

6. SCOPE CAVEATS (do not alter the four figures or the two differences)
(a) Units differ in kind: Row A/B are percentages of the refrigerant charge in the appliance being serviced; Row C/D are percentages of the refrigerant in a laboratory test stand under appendix C. The numeric comparison is apples-to-apples only because the regulation deliberately uses the same 90/80 thresholds for both.
(b) Alternative compliance routes exist and are not captured by the headline percentages: § 82.156(b)(3) permits evacuating the appliance to four inches of mercury vacuum instead of meeting the percentage; § 82.158(e)(2) permits certification of post-1993 equipment on a four-inch vacuum under appendix B1. An appliance serviced under (b)(3), or a device certified only under (e)(2), can be fully compliant without the 90/80 percentage being the operative criterion.
(c) Applicability: these percentages govern small appliances only. MVACs and MVAC-like appliances are governed by § 82.156(c)-(d) (evacuation to 102 mm Hg or subpart B), and other appliance classes by § 82.156(a) Table 1 vacuum levels — none of which are percentage recovery standards.

question: Y109
answer:
ANSWER (Ask 2): No. Under 10 CFR 431.97 as in force on 2026-11-21, the January 1, 2029 minimum efficiency standards for air-cooled commercial package air conditioning and heating equipment do NOT apply to an air-cooled unit with cooling capacity less than 65,000 Btu/h. Such a unit is expressly excluded from the paragraph (b) standards, and the 2029 table is by its own terms limited to equipment with cooling capacity greater than or equal to 65,000 Btu/h.

CONTROLLING SCOPE LANGUAGE (Ask 3) — quoted verbatim.

(1) The operative applicability sentence, 10 CFR 431.97(b), second sentence:

"Each air-cooled commercial package air conditioning and heating equipment (excluding air-cooled equipment with cooling capacity less than 65,000 Btu/h and double-duct air conditioners or heat pumps) manufactured on or after January 1, 2029, must meet the applicable minimum energy efficiency standard level(s) set forth in table 2 to this paragraph (b)."

(2) The parallel sentence for the preceding tier, 10 CFR 431.97(b), first sentence, which contains the identical exclusion:

"Each air-cooled commercial package air conditioning and heating equipment (excluding air-cooled equipment with cooling capacity less than 65,000 Btu/h and double-duct air conditioners or heat pumps) manufactured on or after January 1, 2023, and before January 1, 2029, must meet the applicable minimum energy efficiency standard level(s) set forth in table 1 to this paragraph (b)."

(3) The caption of the table the 2029 sentence incorporates, which independently states the capacity scope:

"Table 2 to Paragraph (b)—Updated Minimum Efficiency Standards for Air-Cooled Commercial Package Air Conditioning and Heating Equipment With a Cooling Capacity Greater Than or Equal to 65,000 Btu/h (Excluding Double-Duct Air Conditioners and Heat Pumps)"

Every capacity row in table 2 begins at or above the threshold: "≥65,000 Btu/h and <135,000 Btu/h," "≥135,000 Btu/h and <240,000 Btu/h," and "≥240,000 Btu/h and <760,000 Btu/h," each with "Compliance date: equipment manufactured starting on . . . January 1, 2029." Table 1 carries the same ≥65,000 Btu/h rows with a January 1, 2023 date. There is no row, footnote, or subcategory in either table for capacity below 65,000 Btu/h.

(4) Where sub-65,000 Btu/h air-cooled equipment actually is regulated — 10 CFR 431.97(i):

"Air-cooled, three-phase, commercial package air conditioning and heating equipment with a cooling capacity of less than 65,000 Btu/h and air-cooled, three-phase variable refrigerant flow multi-split air conditioning and heating equipment with a cooling capacity of less than 65,000 Btu/h manufactured on or after the compliance date listed in tables 18 and 19 to this paragraph (i) must meet the applicable minimum energy efficiency standard level(s) set forth in this paragraph (i)."

Table 19 to paragraph (i) assigns that class a January 1, 2025 compliance date and SEER2/HSPF2 metrics — 13.4 SEER2 (split-system AC, <65,000 Btu/h), 13.4 SEER2 (single-package AC), 14.3 SEER2 / 7.5 HSPF2 (split-system AC+HP), 13.4 SEER2 / 6.7 HSPF2 (single-package AC+HP) — not the IVEC/IVHE metrics and January 1, 2029 date of table 2.

APPLICATION TO THE STATED UNIT.
- Element 1, equipment type: air-cooled commercial package air conditioning and heating equipment — within subpart F.
- Element 2, capacity: less than 65,000 Btu/h — falls squarely inside the parenthetical exclusion in 431.97(b) and outside the "[g]reater than or equal to 65,000 Btu/h" scope of table 2.
- Element 3, date: the 2029 date attaches to equipment "manufactured on or after January 1, 2029" that survives the exclusion; this unit does not survive it.
Result: the 2029 standard is inapplicable. The exclusion and the table-2 capacity limit are exact complements ("less than 65,000 Btu/h" excluded vs. "greater than or equal to 65,000 Btu/h" covered), so there is no gap and no overlap at the 65,000 Btu/h boundary; a unit at exactly 65,000 Btu/h would be covered, one below it is not.

CONDITIONALITY (checked, because a conditional date would change the answer). The January 1, 2029 date in table 2 is unconditional on the face of the text: it is stated as a fixed compliance date in the "Compliance date: equipment manufactured starting on . . ." column, and 431.97(b) imposes the table 2 levels by direct operation of "manufactured on or after January 1, 2029," with no cross-reference to a future rulemaking, determination, or trigger. Nothing in the retrieved text makes the 2029 date contingent. This does not matter to the outcome here, since the unit is excluded before the date is reached, but it confirms the exclusion — not timing — is what controls.

PRACTICE NOTES AND LIMITS OF THE GROUNDING.
1. The standard attaches to the manufacture date ("equipment manufactured on or after"), not to sale, installation, or inventory status.
2. Capacity is rated cooling capacity in Btu/h, as the regulatory text frames it ("cooling capacity"). The threshold is a cooling-capacity threshold, not a heating-capacity or input-capacity threshold; do not substitute input rating.
3. The sub-65,000 Btu/h class in paragraph (i) is expressly "three-phase." If the unit in question is single-phase and below 65,000 Btu/h, it is outside subpart F's small commercial package class altogether and would fall to the consumer-product regime of 10 CFR part 430; the answer to Ask 2 remains No either way, and a fortiori. Confirm phase before citing paragraph (i) as the unit's governing provision.
4. The 431.97(b) sentences are quoted from the codified amendatory text published at 89 FR 44086 (May 20, 2024) (Doc. No. 2024-08546); the table 1/table 2 captions, the ≥65,000 Btu/h row structure, the January 1, 2029 compliance dates, and paragraph (i)/table 19 were confirmed against the eCFR section page and the 2026 print edition of 10 CFR part 431 subpart F (CFR-2026-title10-vol4), both consistent with each other. No amendment between the 2026 edition and the 2026-11-21 as-of date altered the exclusion or the 2029 date in the retrieved text.
5. Adjacent provisions confirm the split rather than disturb it: 10 CFR 429.67 is captioned for "[a]ir-cooled, three-phase, small commercial package air conditioning and heating equipment with a cooling capacity of less than 65,000 British thermal units per hour" and prescribes SEER/SEER2/HSPF certification metrics for that class, and the appendix table for subpart F lists "Air-Cooled, 3-Phase, AC and HP, <65,000 Btu/h" against Appendices F and F1 (SEER and HSPF; SEER2 and HSPF2), while "≥65,000 Btu/h and <760,000 Btu/h" maps to Appendices A and A1 (EER, IEER, COP; EER2, COP2, IVEC, IVHE). The test procedure and metric split tracks the same 65,000 Btu/h line as the standard.

BOTTOM LINE FOR THE FILE: cite 431.97(b)'s parenthetical exclusion ("excluding air-cooled equipment with cooling capacity less than 65,000 Btu/h") and the table 2 caption ("With a Cooling Capacity Greater Than or Equal to 65,000 Btu/h") as the controlling scope language; the January 1, 2029 standard does not apply to the described unit, whose applicable standard is the sub-65,000 Btu/h class standard in 431.97(i) with a January 1, 2025 compliance date.

The first reads: "Table 19 to Paragraph ( i )—Updated Minimum Efficiency Standards for Air-Cooled, Three-Phase, Commercial Package Air Conditioning and Heating Equipment With a Cooling Capacity of Less Than 65,000 Btu/ h and Air-Cooled, Three-Phase, Small Va"

question: Y110
answer:
DETERMINATION

No. Under 10 CFR 430.32 as in force on 2026-11-21, the energy conservation standards in that section do not apply to a refrigerator-freezer whose total refrigerated volume exceeds 39 cubic feet. The controlling scope language is the undesignated introductory text of § 430.32(a), quoted verbatim:

  "(a) Refrigerators/refrigerator-freezers/freezers. These standards do not apply to refrigerators and refrigerator-freezers with total refrigerated volume exceeding 39 cubic feet (1104 liters) or freezers with total refrigerated volume exceeding 30 cubic feet (850 liters). The energy standards as determined by the equations of the following table(s) shall be rounded off to the nearest kWh per year. If the equation calculation is halfway between the nearest two kWh per year values, the standard shall be rounded up to the higher of these values."

1. WHY THIS TEXT CONTROLS

1.1 Placement. The exclusion is not in a product-class row of any table; it is the opening sentence of paragraph (a) itself. Every refrigerator/refrigerator-freezer/freezer standard in § 430.32 — Table 1 to (a)(1) (manufactured on or after Sept 15, 2014 and before the 2029/2030 compliance dates), the (a)(2) standards tied to the 2029/2030 compliance dates by product class, and Table 4 to (a)(3) (manufactured on or after Jan 31, 2030) — sits downstream of that sentence and is subject to it. The exclusion therefore governs regardless of which subparagraph's standard would otherwise be the operative one on a given manufacture date.

1.2 Product-class neutrality. The exclusion is stated for "refrigerators and refrigerator-freezers" as a group. It is not limited to any table row. Accordingly it reaches a refrigerator-freezer of any listed class — manual defrost, partial automatic defrost, automatic defrost with top-, side-, or bottom-mounted freezer, with or without through-the-door ice service or an automatic icemaker, compact, and built-in — provided the total refrigerated volume exceeds 39 ft³.

1.3 The 30 ft³ figure is a different product. The companion "30 cubic feet (850 liters)" cap applies to freezers only. It has no bearing on a refrigerator-freezer.

2. HOW TO APPLY IT (procedure)

Step 1 — Classify the unit as a refrigerator-freezer under 10 CFR 430.2 (a cabinet with a source of refrigeration requiring single-phase AC electric input only, having a compartment capable of maintaining compartment temperatures below 32 °F and a separate compartment capable of maintaining 0 °F or below, as determined per § 429.14(d)(2)). If it is a freezer or an all-refrigerator, a different branch of § 430.32(a) applies; if it is a miscellaneous refrigeration product, Subpart C elsewhere applies.
Step 2 — Determine the unit's TOTAL REFRIGERATED VOLUME (unadjusted fresh-food plus freezer compartment volume), measured per the DOE test procedure for refrigerators/refrigerator-freezers/freezers (10 CFR 430 Subpart B, Appendix A1) and reported per § 429.14. Do not use total adjusted volume (AV) for this test. AV is the input variable in the maximum-energy-use equations; it is not the scope metric. A unit can have an AV that appears in a table while being outside the standards altogether, because AV > total refrigerated volume.
Step 3 — Compare, strictly. If total refrigerated volume > 39 ft³, the § 430.32 standards do not apply — stop; no maximum energy use (kWh/yr) is computed and no § 430.32 compliance date attaches. If total refrigerated volume ≤ 39 ft³, the unit is within the standards and the applicable table row (Table 1 to (a)(1), (a)(2), or Table 4 to (a)(3), keyed to the manufacture date) governs.
Step 4 — Record the basis: measured total refrigerated volume in ft³ (and L), the test procedure used, and the manufacture date.

3. NUMERIC CONSISTENCY AND EDGE CASES (stated so the deliverable does not contradict itself)

3.1 The requester's threshold and the regulation's threshold are identical: 39 cubic feet. The parenthetical "(1104 liters)" is a rounding of 39 ft³ (39 ft³ = 1104.05 L). The regulation is drafted with cubic feet as the operative figure, so 39 ft³ is the controlling bound and 1104 L is its rounded metric companion. The ~0.05 L band between 1104.00 L and 1104.05 L is a de minimis drafting artifact, not a separate standard.
3.2 "Exceeding" is strict. A unit at exactly 39.00 ft³ (1104 L) is NOT excluded — the exclusion requires the volume to be greater than 39 ft³. 39 ft³ is a ceiling on coverage, not a threshold of exclusion at equality.
3.3 The 30 ft³ / 850 L freezer cap converts as 30 ft³ = 849.5 L, consistent with the regulation's "(850 liters)" parenthetical. It is quoted here only for completeness and is not the basis of this answer.
3.4 The requester's fact pattern ("exceeding 39 cubic feet") already satisfies the strict-comparison test in Step 3, so the verdict does not turn on any measurement dispute. If a specific unit's volume were contested, Step 2 would resolve it.

4. CURRENCY OF THE TEXT ON 2026-11-21 (satisfies the ask-1 constraint)

The quoted exclusion sentence was verified verbatim in three independent renderings of § 430.32: (i) the eCFR text of 10 CFR 430.32 retrieved 2026-11-23; (ii) the GovInfo XML of 10 CFR 430.32 from the 2026 edition of title 10 (1-1-26 edition); and (iii) the GovInfo PDF of the same 2026 edition section, which carries the page footer "§ 430.32 10 CFR Ch. II (1–1–26 Edition)". The 2026 print edition reflects amendments effective on or before January 1, 2026; the eCFR retrieval reflects the text in force on 2026-11-23, two days after the operative date, so absent a rule effective in that 48-hour window (none is evidenced) the text is the text in force on 2026-11-21. Nothing in the amendments appearing in paragraph (a) — the 2029/2030 compliance-date standards in (a)(2) and Table 4 to (a)(3) — alters or removes the exclusion sentence; they add standards that the exclusion continues to govern.

5. SCOPE LIMITS OF THIS ANSWER (so it is not over-read)

5.1 This answers only the § 430.32 standards question posed. The exclusion is expressly worded as "These standards do not apply" — i.e., it is an exclusion from the energy conservation standards of § 430.32(a). The quoted text does not say the product is outside every requirement of 10 CFR Part 430, and this answer does not so hold. Whether any test-procedure, certification, or reporting obligation under Subpart B or § 429.14 attaches to a >39 ft³ refrigerator-freezer is a separate question not resolved by this sentence and is not addressed here.
5.2 This is not a statement about commercial refrigeration equipment under 10 CFR Part 431 (which uses different definitions and different thresholds) or about any state requirement. The requester's unit is treated as a consumer product under Part 430, consistent with the § 430.32(a) framing.
5.3 This answers applicability only. Because the standards do not apply, there is no applicable maximum energy use in kWh/yr to compute for this unit; no equation from Table 1, (a)(2), or Table 4 is evaluated.
5.4 The § 430.2 definitions of "refrigerator-freezer" and "total refrigerated volume" were not reproduced in the source material retrieved for this task; the answer therefore does not quote them. The determination is unaffected because the decisive fact (total refrigerated volume exceeding 39 ft³) is supplied by the requester and the controlling scope text is quoted verbatim.

question: Y111
answer:
ANSWER — Pressure Systems Safety Regulations 2000 (SI 2000/128), regulation 8, original version (as made)

Short answer
- Ask 2 — Who must draw up the written scheme of examination or certify it as suitable: a COMPETENT PERSON. The scheme must have been 'drawn up, or certified as being suitable, by a competent person' (reg 8(2)(a)). The party under the legal duty to ensure that this has happened is the user of an installed system or the owner of a mobile system.
- Ask 3 — Who must review its content at appropriate intervals for suitability in current conditions of use: a COMPETENT PERSON. The content must be 'reviewed at appropriate intervals by a competent person for the purpose of determining whether it is suitable in current conditions of use of the system' (reg 8(2)(b)(i)). Again, the party under the duty to ensure the review happens (and that the scheme is modified per the reviewer's recommendations) is the user/owner.

So the same class of actor — 'a competent person' — performs both functions. The regulation does not require the drawer-up/certifier and the reviewer to be different competent persons, nor the same one; it says 'a competent person' in each place.

VERBATIM TEXT OF REGULATION 8 AS MADE

'Written scheme of examination

8.—(1) The user of an installed system and owner of a mobile system shall not operate the system or allow it to be operated unless he has a written scheme for the periodic examination, by a competent person, of the following parts of the system, that is to say–
(a) all protective devices;
(b) every pressure vessel and every pipeline in which (in either case) a defect may give rise to danger; and
(c) those parts of the pipework in which a defect may give rise to danger,
and such parts of the system shall be identified in the scheme.

(2) The said user or owner shall–
(a) ensure that the scheme has been drawn up, or certified as being suitable, by a competent person;
(b) ensure that–
  (i) the content of the scheme is reviewed at appropriate intervals by a competent person for the purpose of determining whether it is suitable in current conditions of use of the system; and
  (ii) the content of the scheme is modified in accordance with any recommendations made by that competent person arising out of that review.

(3) No person shall draw up or certify a scheme of examination under paragraph (2)(a) unless the scheme is suitable and–
(a) specifies the nature and frequency of examination;
(b) specifies any measures necessary to prepare the pressure system for safe examination other than those it would be reasonable to expect the user (in the case of an installed system) or owner (in the case of a mobile system) to take without specialist advice; and
(c) where appropriate, provides for an examination to be carried out before the pressure system is used for the first time.

(4) References in paragraphs (2) and (3) to the suitability of the scheme are references to its suitability for the purposes of preventing danger from those parts of the pressure system included in the scheme.'

Source: https://www.legislation.gov.uk/uksi/2000/128/regulation/8/made (fetched 2026-11-23T11:44:18Z, sha256 58040c6817a3); identical text at .../regulation/8/made/data.xht (sha256 ef83e6d02303) and .../regulation/8/data.html (sha256 96d7c4f13d89), which adds 'Commencement Information I1 Reg. 8 in force at 21.2.2000, see reg. 1'. Corroborated by the 21/02/2000 point-in-time view (.../regulation/8/2000-02-21, sha256 f4431e730ad4) and by the reproduction of reg 8 in HSE L122 'Safety of pressure systems' (sha256 b3f0f7218b0c).

DUTY ALLOCATION TABLE (who must ensure vs who must act)

| Provision | Duty holder — must ensure | Actor — performs the function | Function |
|---|---|---|---|
| 8(1) | user (installed system) / owner (mobile system) | — (prohibition) | Must not operate, or allow operation, without a written scheme for periodic examination by a competent person, covering all protective devices, every pressure vessel and pipeline where a defect may give rise to danger, and those parts of the pipework where a defect may give rise to danger; those parts must be identified in the scheme |
| 8(2)(a) | the said user or owner | a competent person | Draw up the scheme, or certify it as being suitable |
| 8(2)(b)(i) | the said user or owner | a competent person | Review the content of the scheme at appropriate intervals, to determine whether it is suitable in current conditions of use |
| 8(2)(b)(ii) | the said user or owner | — | Modify the content of the scheme in accordance with any recommendations made by that competent person arising out of the review |
| 8(3) | any person who draws up or certifies under 8(2)(a) | that person | Prohibition on drawing up or certifying unless the scheme is suitable and specifies (a) nature and frequency of examination, (b) measures necessary to prepare the system for safe examination beyond what the user/owner could reasonably be expected to take without specialist advice, and (c) where appropriate, a pre-first-use examination |
| 8(4) | — | — | 'Suitability' in 8(2) and 8(3) means suitability for preventing danger from the parts of the system included in the scheme |

POINTS A COMPLIANCE READER NEEDS ON THE FACE OF THIS ANSWER

1. Two distinct legal persons in every limb of reg 8(2): the duty holder ('the said user or owner') and the competent actor. Reg 8(2) is drafted as 'ensure that …', not as a direct obligation on the user/owner to write or review the scheme personally. Answering 'the user' or 'the owner' to asks 2 and 3 would be wrong as to who performs the function, though right as to who is answerable for it being done.

2. Installed vs mobile systems. Reg 8(1)–(2) split the duty holder: 'the user of an installed system and owner of a mobile system'. Reg 8(3)(b) carries the same split into the content requirement. The identity of the duty holder therefore depends on which category the system falls into; the actor (competent person) does not vary.

3. Certification route. Reg 8(2)(a) is disjunctive: 'drawn up, or certified as being suitable, by a competent person'. A scheme may be drafted by someone who is not a competent person provided a competent person certifies it as suitable. HSE L122 confirms this at paragraphs 95–96: 'Where the written scheme of examination is written by someone other than a competent person, it must be certified as suitable by a competent person'; 'The written scheme of examination should be drawn up by a competent person, or if drawn up by someone other than a competent person, certified as suitable by a competent person.' Note, though, that reg 8(3) is addressed to 'No person' who draws up or certifies: whatever the author's status, the scheme must satisfy 8(3)(a)–(c) and be suitable within reg 8(4).

4. Review timing. The regulation fixes no interval; it says 'at appropriate intervals'. The regulation does not require the reviewer to be independent of the examination function, and does not prevent the same competent person who drew up the scheme from reviewing it. HSE L122 para 116 states the responsibility point in the same terms as the regulation: 'It is the user's/owner's responsibility under the Regulations to ensure that the content of the written scheme is reviewed periodically by a competent person.'

5. 'As made' caveat (ask 1). The text above is taken from the legislation.gov.uk version labelled 'Original (As Enacted or Made)', whose own status note reads: 'This is the original version (as it was originally made). No changes have been applied to the text.' It is confirmed against the 21/02/2000 point-in-time view, which records: 'There are currently no known outstanding effects for The Pressure Systems Safety Regulations 2000, Section 8.' No later amendment has been applied or relied on anywhere in this answer; the answer is therefore valid for reg 8 as made on 21 February 2000 and does not purport to state the current consolidated text.

6. Deliberately not asserted (grounding limit, not a gap in the answer to asks 2 and 3). The Regulations define 'competent person', 'user', 'owner', 'installed system' and 'mobile system' in regulation 2. Those definitions were not present in the fetched passages and are therefore not quoted or paraphrased here; anyone needing the statutory test of competence or the statutory identification of user/owner should read regulation 2 of SI 2000/128 directly. Nothing in asks 2 or 3 turns on that wording: each ask is answered by the express words of reg 8(2)(a) and 8(2)(b)(i), both of which name 'a competent person'.

7. Scope note. Reg 8 applies to systems within the Regulations; the Regulations' exclusions and threshold provisions (which determine whether a given system is in scope at all) are outside the text of reg 8 and are not addressed here, because the asks concern who performs the two functions once reg 8 applies.

question: Y112
answer:
THOROUGH-EXAMINATION INTERVALS UNDER THE ORIGINAL (AS MADE) LOLER 1998, REGULATION 9 AND SCHEDULE 1

1. Governing text (constraint — ask 1)

Source: The Lifting Operations and Lifting Equipment Regulations 1998, S.I. 1998/2307, regulation 9(3), read in the as-made ('Original') version, i.e. the text in force at commencement on 5 December 1998 (legislation.gov.uk plain view of reg 9 as at 1998-12-05), together with Schedule 1 paragraph 7 as made. The as-made text is materially identical to the current revised text for the provisions in question; the only textual amendments recorded against regulation 9 are F1 (S.I. 2019/696, in force 31.12.2020, reg 9(1)(b)), F2 (S.I. 2016/1093, in force 8.12.2016, reg 9(1)(b)), F3 (S.I. 2014/3248, in force 6.4.2015, reg 9(5)) and F4 (S.I. 2013/448, in force 6.4.2013, reg 9(7)(b)). None of them touches regulation 9(3)(a)(i) or (ii). The as-made wording of reg 9(1)(b) reads '...an EC declaration of conformity could or (in the case of a declaration under the Lifts Regulations 1997) should have been drawn up...', which confirms the 1998-12-05 version is the as-made one.

Regulation 9(3), as made, provides (verbatim):

'(3) Subject to paragraph (6), every employer shall ensure that lifting equipment which is exposed to conditions causing deterioration which is liable to result in dangerous situations is—
 (a) thoroughly examined—
   (i) in the case of lifting equipment for lifting persons or an accessory for lifting, at least every 6 months;
   (ii) in the case of other lifting equipment, at least every 12 months; or
   (iii) in either case, in accordance with an examination scheme; and
   (iv) each time that exceptional circumstances which are liable to jeopardise the safety of the lifting equipment have occurred; and
 (b) if appropriate for the purpose, is inspected by a competent person at suitable intervals between thorough examinations,
 to ensure that health and safety conditions are maintained and that any deterioration can be detected and remedied in good time.'

Schedule 1 paragraph 7 (as made) corroborates both figures by requiring the report of a thorough examination to state whether the examination is:
'(i) within an interval of 6 months under regulation 9(3)(a)(i);
 (ii) within an interval of 12 months under regulation 9(3)(a)(ii);
 (iii) in accordance with an examination scheme under regulation 9(3)(a)(iii); or
 (iv) after the occurrence of exceptional circumstances under regulation 9(3)(a)(iv);'

Note on scope: Schedule 1 does not itself set intervals — it prescribes the information a report of thorough examination must contain (reg 10(1)). The intervals live in regulation 9(3); Schedule 1 para 7 merely reproduces them for reporting purposes. The two sources are consistent, so the answer is not sensitive to which is read.

2. Interval for lifting equipment for lifting persons, or an accessory for lifting (ask 2)

6 months — a maximum interval: the examination must be carried out 'at least every 6 months'. Applies to both (a) lifting equipment for lifting persons and (b) an accessory for lifting (e.g. slings, shackles, lifting beams, swivel hoist rings), regardless of whether persons are lifted.

3. Interval for other lifting equipment (ask 3)

12 months — a maximum interval: 'at least every 12 months'. This is the residual category: lifting equipment that is neither equipment for lifting persons nor a lifting accessory (e.g. standard fork-lift trucks, workshop cranes, goods-only hoists).

4. Difference (ask 4)

12 months − 6 months = 6 months. The persons/accessory interval is 6 months shorter than the other-equipment interval. Arithmetic check: 6 + 6 = 12, and 6 < 12, so the stated difference is consistent with both stated maxima and does not exceed either.

5. Tabulated result

| Category (reg 9(3)(a)) | As-made interval | Nature of limit | Months |
| Lifting equipment for lifting persons, or an accessory for lifting — 9(3)(a)(i) | every 6 months | maximum | 6 |
| Other lifting equipment — 9(3)(a)(ii) | every 12 months | maximum | 12 |
| Difference (12 − 6) | — | — | 6 |

6. Safety-engineering caveats a duty-holder must carry alongside these numbers

(a) These are maxima, not fixed periods. 'At least every X months' means the examination must occur no later than X months after the previous one; a competent person may specify a shorter interval, and an employer must follow it.
(b) Regulation 9(3)(a)(iii) permits an 'examination scheme' in place of the 6/12-month rule, 'in either case'. A scheme may therefore produce shorter intervals but cannot lawfully extend beyond what is safe; where a scheme is used, the Schedule 1 para 7 report must say so (para 7(a)(iii)) rather than citing the 6- or 12-month limb.
(c) Regulation 9(3) is expressly 'Subject to paragraph (6)': for equipment already subject to a pre-1998 statutory examination requirement listed in reg 9(7) (Factories Act 1961, Shipbuilding and Ship-repairing 1960, Construction (Lifting Operations) 1961, Offices Shops and Railway Premises (Hoists and Lifts) 1968, Offshore Installations 1976, Docks 1988), the first examination under reg 9(3) had to be made before the date the old provision would have required it — a transitional first-cycle rule that can shorten the first interval only.
(d) Regulation 9(3)(a)(iv) adds an event-driven examination after any exceptional circumstance liable to jeopardise safety; this is additional to, and unaffected by, the periodic intervals above.
(e) Regulation 9(2) imposes separate examinations after installation and after assembly at a new site/location, and reg 9(1) a pre-first-use examination — neither is a substitute for the periodic 6/12-month regime.
(f) The 6-month classification follows function, not the label on the equipment: a chain sling is an 'accessory for lifting' at 6 months; the same chain used as a fixed strop in a non-lifting role is outside LOLER entirely. Misclassification here is the commonest cause of an overdue examination.

7. Answer stated plainly

Under the original (as made) LOLER 1998, reg 9(3)(a)(i): 6 months for lifting equipment for lifting persons or an accessory for lifting. Reg 9(3)(a)(ii): 12 months for other lifting equipment. The first interval is 6 months shorter than the second. Schedule 1 para 7(a)(i)–(ii) reproduces the same 6-month and 12-month figures, confirming the reading.

question: Y113
answer:
STORM FREQUENCY CRITERIA — FHWA HYDRAULIC DESIGN SERIES NO. 4, "DESIGN OF ROADSIDE CHANNELS"

=====================================================================
1. ANSWER
=====================================================================

| Facility (Interstate System projects)                                   | Design storm frequency |
|-------------------------------------------------------------------------|------------------------|
| Drainage facilities OTHER THAN culverts and bridges                     | 10-year                |
| Underpass or other depressed roadway where ponded water can be removed  | 50-year                |
|   ONLY through the storm-drain system                                   |                        |

Restated as the rule reads: the minimum is a 10-year frequency, and the 50-year frequency is the mandatory exception (a higher, rarer event) at sag/underpass/depressed locations with no gravity relief other than the storm drain.

=====================================================================
2. SOURCE TEXT (verbatim, with citation)
=====================================================================

HDS-4, Design of Roadside Channels, Federal Highway Administration (successor to the Bureau of Public Roads), May 1965, Chapter 2 (Estimating Storm Runoff from Small Areas) — discussion of design frequency preceding/within Section 2.2, "Storm Runoff." Author: James K. Searcy, FHWA Bridge Division.

Quoted text as it appears in the PDF (OCR artifacts marked):

"...on minor highways where serious erosion damage would result from overtopping the drainage channels, a less frequent peak runoff might be used as the design runoff. The frequency used depends somewhat upon the climate, the topography of the area, and the cost of the drainage system. Water standing on the edge of the traveled way for a few minutes during an intense storm might not interfere with traffic movement any more than the storm itself, but should water remain for a long time or collect in pavement sags or in underpass depressions, a traffic hazard will result. At locations where shoulder gutters protect high fills highly susceptible to erosion, the peak discharge for which the channels are designed might be greater than the class of the road would otherwise warrant.

Bureau of Public Roads policy requires that on Interstate System projects, a[ll] drainage facilities other than culverts and bridges be designed to keep the traveled ways usable during storms at least as great as that for a 10-year frequency, except that a 50-year frequency shall be used for underpass or other depressed roadways where ponded water can be removed only through the storm-drain system."

Cleaning notes: the OCR renders "all" as "an" and inserts a stray character ("designedCto") in the phrase "be designed to keep"; these are scan/ conversion artifacts and are corrected above without altering meaning. The document carries its own disclaimer that text was kept as close to the original as possible during electronic conversion.

=====================================================================
3. SCOPE OF EACH VALUE — WHAT IS AND IS NOT COVERED
=====================================================================

10-year criterion applies to (HDS-4 facility types, Ch. 1 taxonomy):
  - Roadside channels and toe-of-slope channels
  - Intercepting channels and median swales
  - Chutes and channel changes/relocations
  - Gutters and shoulder gutters
  - Pavement drainage, inlets, and storm-drain systems on grade (non-sag)
  - Any other drainage facility that is neither a culvert nor a bridge

50-year criterion applies to:
  - Underpasses (highway-rail and highway-highway)
  - Other depressed roadway sections
  CONDITION: ponded water can be removed ONLY through the storm-drain system — i.e., no gravity outfall, no overland relief, no pump-free escape path. The controlling hazard is ponding depth at a low point, not the facility type per se. Where a depressed section has gravity relief at the low point, the 50-year exception does not attach and the 10-year minimum governs.

Explicitly excluded from both values:
  - Culverts (governed by HDS-5, Hydraulic Design of Highway Culverts)
  - Bridges (governed by HDS-7 / HEC-18 and the FHWA bridge design-flood policy; not by this sentence of HDS-4)

=====================================================================
4. EDITION / CURRENCY DETERMINATION
=====================================================================

The 10-year/50-year Interstate rule is a first-edition (May 1965) Bureau of Public Roads policy statement. Edition history, per the FHWA Hydraulics library listing and the acknowledgements of the later edition:
  - 1st ed., May 1965 — "Design of Roadside Channels" (GPO Stock No. 050-001-00068-7); the edition containing the sentence quoted above. Archived.
  - 2nd ed., June 1997 — FHWA-HI-97-028, retitled "Introduction to Highway Hydraulics"; complete rewrite adding closed conduits, energy dissipators.
  - Later printing 2001 — FHWA-NHI-01-019; SI version 1997 — FHWA-HI-97-028; current successor 2008 — FHWA-NHI-08-090.

Currency check — the values are stable across editions:
  (a) The 1997/2008 successor edition (HDS-4 Introduction to Highway Hydraulics) states: "Pavement drainage is normally designed for the 10-year flood, except in sag vertical curves where water cannot escape other than through a storm drain. In these locations, a 50-year event is often used for design to prevent ponding to a depth that could drown people if they were to drive into it."
  (b) HEC-12, Drainage of Highway Pavements, Sec. 3.1, independently confirms the policy: "The design frequency usually used in the design of depressed sections and underpasses is greatly influenced by Federal Highway Administration policy which has required the use of a 50-year frequency for underpasses and depressed sections on Interstate highways where ponded water can be removed only through the storm drain system. This policy has also been widely used at similar locations for other highways."

Conclusion: no edition of HDS-4 conflicts with the 10-year/50-year answer. The numbers are not superseded.

=====================================================================
5. APPLICATION PROCEDURE
=====================================================================

Step 1 — Classify the facility. Is it a culvert, a bridge, or "other"? If culvert or bridge, stop; use HDS-5 or HDS-7 respectively.

Step 2 — Determine the route classification. Is the project on the Interstate System? If yes, the 10-year floor is mandatory, not discretionary. If no (NHS, State, local), HDS-4 leaves frequency to engineering judgment based on climate, topography, cost, erosion consequence, and traffic disruption — the 10-year/50-year pair is a floor for Interstate work and a widely adopted benchmark elsewhere.

Step 3 — Test for the depressed-roadway exception. Ask: at the low point (sag vertical curve, underpass, depressed section), can ponded water leave by any path other than the storm-drain system (gravity outfall, overflow swale, sheet relief over a shoulder)?
   - No relief except the storm drain → design to the 50-year event.
   - Relief exists → 10-year minimum governs; apply the 50-year as a CHECK event against ponding depth.

Step 4 — Apply the design event. Size inlets, storm drains, and the outlet for the 50-year peak discharge at depressed/underpass locations; size on-grade channels, gutters, and inlets for the 10-year peak. Runoff determined per HDS-4 Ch. 2 (Rational Method: Q = CiA, with time of concentration and intensity-duration-frequency data).

Step 5 — Check-storm verification at critical locations. Even where 50-year is the design event, run a rarer event to confirm the ponding depth does not create a drowning/vehicle-stall hazard, and confirm that at least one lane remains open (a standard check-event criterion). HDS-4's rationale is explicit: the hazard is water that "remain[s] for a long time or collect[s] in pavement sags or in underpass depressions."

Step 6 — Frequency-analysis convention. HDS-4 Ch. 2 notes that for return periods under 10 years the partial-duration series is more appropriate than the annual series; conversion factors given are 2-yr ×1.13, 5-yr ×1.04, 10-yr ×1.01, 20-yr or more ×1.00. At 10 years and above (both of the governing frequencies here), the two series are effectively interchangeable — no adjustment needed for the 10-year or 50-year design storms.

=====================================================================
6. CAVEATS FOR THE DESIGNER
=====================================================================

- The 1965 HDS-4 language is BPR/FHWA policy as of that edition. State DOT drainage manuals commonly carry the same 10-year/50-year pair (often as 10-year for pavement/storm drains and 50-year or greater for sag points and depressed sections), sometimes with a check storm at 100-year. Verify the governing State DOT manual and any project-specific design criteria; where a State criterion is more stringent, the more stringent value controls.
- The 50-year value is a design frequency at depressed locations under this policy, not merely a check event; HEC-12 also describes the practice of using the 50-year as a check storm for series of inlets terminating at a sag. Both usages are consistent with the HDS-4 rule and are not alternatives to it.
- The rule says "at least as great as" for the 10-year — a 25-year design for an erosion-critical channel is compliant; a 5-year design is not, on Interstate work.
